title: Anytime-Valid Conformal Risk Control
claim: Standard calibration guarantees fail at many sample sizes; anytime-valid correction keeps risk below target across all sample sizes with high probability.
layout: 3 panels left-to-right, shared x-axis, red/green line colors, dashed target line
description: Three side-by-side line plots share the x-axis 'Calibration sample size' on a log scale from about 10^2 to 10^6. The y-axis is miscoverage rate in percent, and a dashed blue horizontal line marks the 5% target. Each plot overlays many thin trajectories, one per calibration draw. Panel (a), 'Standard method', is almost entirely red. Its curves start high and noisy at small n, with values up to 25, and cross the target line before converging to it. Panel (b), 'Fixed-time valid, δ=10%', mixes red and green. Its curves rise from below and some exceed the target at moderate n. Panel (c), 'Anytime-valid, δ=10%', is almost entirely green. Its curves approach 5% from below, with only a few red lines. The eye goes first to the red-to-green color shift across the panels.
caption: Miscoverage rates of prediction sets {Cn(X)} versus calibration sample size n. Each line corresponds to a particular draw of calibration data and the miscoverage rates are evaluated conditional on this data at each n. A green line indicates that all the rates fall below α = 5%, while red indicates a failure. Details are given in Section 5.
abstract: Prediction sets provide a means of quantifying the uncertainty in predictive tasks. Using held out calibration data, conformal prediction and risk control can produce prediction sets that exhibit statistically valid error control in a computationally efficient manner. However, in the standard formulations, the error is only controlled on average over many possible calibration datasets of fixed size. In this paper, we extend the control to remain valid with high probability over a cumulatively growing calibration dataset at any time point. We derive such guarantees using quantile-based arguments and illustrate the applicability of the proposed framework to settings involving distribution shift. We further show that our guarantees are asymptotically tight, in the sense that the risks converge to the target level from below, and that the rate of our correction cannot be improved. Finally, we demonstrate the practical performance of our methods through both simulations and real-world numerical examples.
